abstract: Abstract Background Chimeric antigen receptor (CAR) T-cell therapy has shown notable advancements in the treatment of solid tumors. Nevertheless, its effectiveness is limited to a small group of patients, highlighting the need for predictive biomarkers. This study aimed to investigate biomarkers associated with the efficacy of CAR-T therapy in hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC). Methods We prospectively collected plasma samples from 17 patients with HCC before and after they underwent CAR-glypican-3 (GPC3) T-cell therapy as part of three clinical trials. Plasma proteomic profiling was conducted by using liquid chromatography-mass spectrometry. We examined sequential plasma samples to evaluate the impact of CAR T-cell therapy on the systemic plasma proteome. Additionally, we compared the pretreatment plasma protein profiles between groups with and without clinical benefit (CB) to identify proteins linked to treatment efficacy. The Cox proportional hazard model was used to evaluate the relationship between plasma protein levels and survival outcomes. Results Among 5337 plasma proteins, 225 exhibited significant changes following CAR-GPC3 T-cell therapy. The CB group showed an increased expression in proteins related to the type I interferon signaling pathway, T-cell proliferation and activation, tumor necrosis factor production, and antigen processing and presentation. In addition, plasma proteins were significantly associated with survival outcomes, whereas no significant association was observed between clinical variables and prognosis. Conclusions Plasma proteomics not only captured CAR-GPC3-driven plasma microenvironment remodeling but also identified baseline proteins predictive of CB and survival, which were superior to clinical variables, thus constituting a candidate biomarker panel for HCC patient selection and response monitoring.

Patients and methods
Patient characteristics and sample collection
This study included patients from three phase I clinical trials of CAR-GPC3 T-cell therapy (
NCT03884751
,
NCT03980288
, and
NCT04756648
). The patients enrolled in these trials were required to have a histological diagnosis of HCC with GPC3 expression on tumor cells (≥1+ intensity by immunohistochemistry in any percentage of tumor cells). During these phase I studies, we prospectively collected plasma samples at baseline and 1 week after CAR-GPC3 T-cell therapy for future biomarker analysis. The blood samples were centrifuged within 1 h of collection, and the plasma was stored at −80°C for further analysis. Pretreatment baseline plasma was available for all 17 patients; paired plasma samples were collected from 14 patients 1 week posttreatment. Clinical variables, including age, sex, previous treatment modalities, tumor burden, extrahepatic metastasis, vascular invasion, Child-Pugh score, alpha-fetoprotein (AFP) level, neutrophil-to-lymphocyte ratio (NLR), and C-reactive protein (CRP) level, were also reviewed. The study adhered to the ethical guidelines of the 1975 Declaration of Helsinki and was approved by the Institutional Review Board of the First Affiliated Hospital, Zhejiang University School of Medicine (approval number: IIT20240092B).
Tumor response was assessed using the Response Evaluation Criteria in Solid Tumors (RECIST) version 1.1. Contrast-enhanced computed tomography (CT) or magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) was performed to assess the tumor response every 4 weeks during the first 6 months after CAR-GPC3 T-cell therapy and thereafter every 6 weeks. The patients were categorized into clinical benefit (CB) and non-clinical benefit (NCB) groups based on the Society for Immunotherapy of Cancer’s (SITC) definition of resistance to immunotherapy [
16
]. The CB group included patients who achieved complete response (CR), partial response (PR), or stable disease for more than 6 months before disease progression. The NCB group included patients who did not achieve CR or PR and experienced disease progression within 6 months of initial CAR-GPC3 T-cell therapy. PFS was calculated from the date of the first infusion of CAR-GPC3 T cells to the date of disease progression or death. Overall survival (OS) was defined as the period from the start of CAR T-cell therapy to death or the last follow-up. The study design is illustrated in
Figure 1A
.
Figure 1.
Serially collected plasma samples and clinical outcomes of patients with HCC receiving CAR-GPC3 T-cell therapy in this study. (A) Overview of the study design. Paired plasma samples were collected before and after the infusion of CAR-T cells and subjected to proteomic analysis. (B) The swimmers’ plot for the treatment responses of 17 patients with HCC enrolled in the study. Based on the RECIST v1.1, three patients showed partial response, and clinical benefits (CB) were evident in six according to the CB criteria defined in this study, which included the time factor. (C) The survival curves of patients with CB and no clinical benefit (NCB). The CB group had significantly longer progression-free survival (PFS) than the NCB group. (D) The overall survival (OS) of the CB group showed a positive trend compared to the NCB group. (E) Forest plots showing the association between clinical variables and survival outcomes. No significant association was found between clinical variables and PFS or OS (F). HCC = hepatocellular carcinoma, CAR = chimeric antigen receptor, GPC3 = glypican-3, LC-MS/MS = liquid chromatography tandem mass spectrometry, RECIST v1.1 = Response Evaluation Criteria in Solid Tumors version 1.1, CB = clinical benefits, NCB = no clinical benefit, PFS = progression-free survival, OS = overall survival, AFP = alpha-fetoprotein, NLR = neutrophil-to-lymphocyte ratio, CRP = C-reactive protein.
Proteomic measurement
An n-LAPE/MS TM Kit (ProteinT Biotechnology Co., Ltd.) was used for plasma enrichment. For sample preparation, 40 µL of plasma was mixed with 260 µL of binding buffer and 10 µL of premixed beads. Subsequently, the samples were incubated at 37°C for 10 min with agitation at 1,000 r/min. After incubation, the samples were centrifuged at 12,000 ×
g
for 5 min to remove the unbound proteins from the supernatant. The enriched beads were then washed three times with 500 µL washing buffer and centrifuged. These beads were resuspended in 50 µL of lysis buffer containing tris(2-carboxyethyl)phosphine hydrochloride (TCEP) and chloroacetamide (CAA), and were heated at 95°C for 10 min with agitation. After cooling to room temperature, trypsin digestion buffer (2 µL) was added, and the mixture was incubated at 37°C for 4 h with shaking. The peptides were precipitated by using 950 µL of acetonitrile (ACN) and were desalted by using the SP3 method on beads. Finally, the peptides were eluted with 20 µL of elution buffer, and their concentrations were measured using Nanodrop for subsequent mass spectrometry (MS) analysis.
An identical amount of iRT sourced from Biognosys was incorporated into each data-dependent acquisition (DDA) or data-independent acquisition (DIA) run by using the Thermo Scientific U3000 nanoflow LC system paired with the Q Exactive HF MS. Peptides were dissolved in a loading buffer containing 2% ACN and were separated on a column measuring 150 µm ID × 30 cm (C18, 1.9 µm, 120 Å, Dr Maisch GmbH) by using a 30-min gradient (A: 2% ACN, 0.1% formic acid [FA]; B: 80% ACN, 0.1% FA; 0–5 min, 3%–6% B; 6–44 min, 6%–90% B; 45–54 min, 90% B; 55–60 min, 6% B) at a flow rate of 600 nL/min. The ion transfer tube was maintained at 270°C, and the spray voltage was set to 2,000 V. A 120 K resolution MS scan at 200 m/z was conducted for DDA, followed by the activation of the top 40 precursors. Using an orbitrap mass analyzer (350–1,500 m/z), the MS AGC target value was set at 3 × 10
6
or a maximum injection time of 40 ms Additionally, with higher-energy C-trap dissociation (HCD) fragmentation at a resolution of 15,000 at 200 m/z, the MS/MS AGC target value was established at 5 × 10
4
or a maximum injection time of 40 ms For DIA, a 60 K resolution MS scan at 200 m/z was employed, and with the Orbitrap mass analyzer (350–1,500 m/z), the AGC target value was set at 1 × 10
6
or a maximum injection time of 20 ms The MS/MS AGC target was configured at 1 × 10
6
, with automatic adjustment of the maximum injection time achieved through HCD fragmentation at a resolution of 30,000 at 200 m/z. The normalized collision energy was set at 28% for both DDA and DIA. In proteome DIA MS runs, the fragmentation analysis was divided into 40 DIA isolation windows, with widths determined based on the DDA search results. MS scans were conducted before each DIA cycle.
Statistical analysis
Clinical covariates and protein biomarkers were examined to identify potential links between the effectiveness of CAR-GPC3 T-cell therapy and the prognosis of patients with HCC. DIA data were analyzed by using DIA-NN (v1.8.1) in the human UniProt database. A 1% false discovery rate (FDR) was established as the cutoff for identifying peptides and proteins. Proteins quantified in at least 80% of all samples were chosen for further analysis. The median normalization method was used for normalization, and missing values were imputed at 1,000. To investigate the changes in plasma proteins during CAR-GPC3 T-cell therapy, protein levels in plasma samples before and after treatment were compared by using a paired two-sided
t
-test. The log2-fold change (log2-FC) was calculated to measure changes in plasma protein levels during treatment. Plasma proteins in the matched pre- and posttreatment samples were further compared using a paired two-sided
t
-test in the separate states of CB and NCB. Additionally, the log2-FC in the CB group was compared with that in the NCB group using a two-sided unpaired
t
-test to identify predictive biomarkers for the treatment efficiency of CAR-GPC3 T-cell therapy. Differentially expressed proteins (DEPs) were defined as those with an adjusted
P
-value of less than 0.05. The “clusterProfiler” package (version 4.10.0) was used to perform Gene Ontology (GO) and Kyoto Encyclopedia of Genes and Genomes (KEGG) analyses [
17
]. Furthermore, human protein–protein interactions (PPIs) were obtained from the STRING database (
https://string-db.org
) for the comprehensive analysis and annotation of protein functional interactions. The PPI network was visualized by using Cytoscape (
https://cytoscape.org
).
The Kaplan–Meier method with log-rank test was used to compare PFS and OS between the CB and NCB groups. To evaluate the influence of clinical variables and plasma proteins on PFS and OS, the Cox proportional hazards model was used. Hazard ratios (HR) were determined by using the Cox regression model. Statistical significance was defined as a two-tailed
P
-value below 0.05. All analyses were conducted using the R software version 4.3.1.

Introduction
Liver cancer is the third most common cause of cancer-related death, with hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) accounting for 75%–85% of these cases [
1
]. Although combination therapies based on programmed death-1 (PD-1) blockade have significantly enhanced treatment outcomes, most patients with HCC eventually develop drug resistance, resulting in a median progression-free survival (PFS) of less than 7 months [
2–4
]. Despite progress in subsequent treatments, effective salvage options for HCC remain scarce, contributing to a 5-year survival rate of less than 20% [
5
]. Recently, chimeric antigen receptor (CAR) T-cell therapy has emerged as a promising immunotherapy owing to its success in treating hematologic cancers [
6
,
7
]. However, solid tumors tend to respond poorly to CAR T-cell therapy, likely because of the immunosuppressive microenvironment and absence of highly specific tumor antigens [
8
].
In contrast to traditional targeted or antibody therapies, CAR T cells are engineered and expanded from peripheral blood T cells to express CAR, thereby enabling them to recognize and attack cells with specific antigens. Glypican-3 (GPC3) is a protein anchored to the cell surface by glycophosphatidylinositol, predominantly and specifically found in HCC cells, whereas its presence in normal tissues is minimal [
9
]. Additionally, the pro-tumoral characteristics of GPC3 have been linked to poor prognosis in patients with HCC [
10
]. Numerous ongoing clinical trials involving CAR T cells have targeted GPC3 for HCC treatment, with positive outcomes reported even in patients who have undergone extensive prior treatment [
11
,
12
]. Our previous prospective clinical trial also demonstrated that CAR-GPC3 T-cell therapy offers a manageable safety profile and promising therapeutic benefits for patients with advanced HCC [
13
]. However, some patients with HCC do not experience the clinical benefits of CAR-GPC3 T cells. Therefore, identifying reliable biomarkers to predict the effectiveness of CAR-GPC3 T-cell therapy is essential for advancing precise cancer immunotherapy and gaining a deep understanding of the mechanisms underlying sensitivity and resistance. Although profiling tumor tissue is crucial for biomarker detection, it has limitations, such as spatial-temporal heterogeneity and limited accessibility. Therefore, identifying biomarkers in peripheral blood samples is crucial for broadening their clinical applications. With advancements in genomics, the study of proteins, known as the “executors of life,” offers additional insights into real-time tumor biology. Research has shown the predictive value of serum proteomic signatures for PD-1 blockade in melanoma and lung cancer [
14
]. However, the dynamic changes and predictive value of serum proteomics in CAR T-cell therapy for solid tumors remain largely unexplored. Recently, a method utilizing the formation of a plasma protein corona on zeolite NaY was developed to deeply profile the plasma proteome, which is capable of detecting approximately 4,000 proteins and 31,000 peptides in a single plasma sample [
15
].
In this study, we aimed to evaluate comprehensive changes in the plasma proteome of patients with HCC undergoing CAR-GPC3 T-cell therapy using prospectively collected sequential plasma samples. Additionally, we identified potential protein biomarkers to predict which patients with HCC could benefit from CAR-GPC3 T-cell therapy for the first time.

Results
Patient characteristics and survival outcomes
Between September 2019 and August 2022, we prospectively collected sequential plasma samples from 17 patients with advanced-stage HCC who were undergoing CAR-GPC3 T-cell therapy across three clinical trials [
13
,
18
,
19
]. The baseline patient characteristics are summarized in
Table 1
. All the patients had chronic hepatitis B virus infection, with no cases of hepatitis C virus or metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease. Of these patients, 15 (88.2%) were males, with a median age of 48 years (range, 23–74 years). Among the 17 patients included in this study, 14 were identified to have extrahepatic metastases, including lung metastases (14 patients), peritoneal metastases (6 patients), and abdominal wall metastasis (1 patient). All patients had an Eastern Cooperative Oncology Group performance status of 0. All participants had previously undergone surgical resection, locoregional therapy, or systemic treatment; however, they experienced disease progression and extrahepatic metastases. Among the 17 patients, 14 underwent curative surgical resection for HCC (2 via open surgery and 12 via laparoscopic resection); the remaining 3 patients did not undergo curative liver resection due to the following reasons: pulmonary metastases at initial diagnosis, multiple intrahepatic metastatic lesions, and diaphragmatic invasion identified during laparoscopic exploration.

Two patients exhibited vascular invasion: one in the CB group and the other in the NCB group. Prior to the infusion of CAR-GPC3 T cells, all patients received lymphodepletion treatment, which included cyclophosphamide and fludarabine for 3 days. The median dose of CAR-GPC3 T cells administered was 2.5 × 10
8
per session. According to the pre-defined classes, the treatment efficacy of three patients (17.6%) was categorized as PR, and six patients (35.3%) were categorized as CB (
Figure 1B
). The median PFS and OS were 3.8 and 9.4 months in the CB group and NCB group, respectively. The CB group demonstrated a significantly longer PFS than the NCB group (
Figure 1C
). Additionally, there was a favorable trend toward extended OS in the CB group (
Figure 1D
). No significant association was found between clinical variables, such as sex, age, prior treatment history, tumor burden, vascular invasion, AFP, NLR, CRP, and PFS or OS (
Figure 1E and F
).
Changes in plasma protein levels during CAR-GPC3 T-cell therapy
To investigate the effects of CAR-GPC3 T-cell therapy on plasma proteins, we examined the changes in plasma proteomics by comparing samples taken before and after treatment with a median interval of 7 days. We analyzed 31 plasma samples from 17 HCC patients who received CAR-GPC3 T-cell infusions, including 14 paired samples before and after therapy. Overall, we identified 5,337 proteins in the samples and focused on those observed in at least 80% of the cases. Initially, we evaluated the overall alterations in plasma proteins during CAR-GPC3 T-cell therapy, independent of the benefits of the treatment. Among patients with HCC treated with CAR-GPC3 T cells, 225 proteins showed significant changes in plasma levels during therapy (
P
< 0.05, |log2-FC| > 1). GNLY, LGALS9, and CXCL11 were the top three proteins with the most significant increase posttreatment, whereas HAMP and TAC3 showed the most notable decrease in plasma levels (
P
< 0.001) (
Figure 2A
). The top 20 proteins with the greatest changes are shown in bar charts based on paired plasma samples (
Figure 2B
).

We conducted GO analyses of the upregulated and downregulated proteins after treatment to investigate the effects of CAR-GPC3 T-cell therapy on biological functions. Most of the altered proteins were enriched in the immune system processes. The proteins that were upregulated after CAR-GPC3 T-cell therapy were primarily linked to the type I interferon (IFN) response, T-cell proliferation and activation, mononuclear cell proliferation, and tumor necrosis factor (TNF) production (
Figure 2C
). In contrast, downregulated proteins were enriched in complement activation, humoral immune response, B-cell-mediated immunity, and immunoglobulin-mediated immune response (
Figure 2D
). We also assessed the plasma protein changes during treatment in the CB and NCB groups. The plasma proteome profiles showed different patterns after CAR-GPC3 T-cell therapy between the CB and NCB groups. Most proteins with significant changes in the CB group did not show any significant changes in the NCB group. A detailed overview of the altered proteins in different groups is provided in
Supplementary Figure S1
.
Pretreatment biomarkers for predicting clinical benefits
To identify potential predictive biomarkers for clinical benefits prior to CAR-GPC3 T-cell therapy, we compared the pretreatment plasma protein levels between the CB and NCB groups. We found that the pretreatment plasma levels of 444 proteins were significantly different between the two groups (
P
< 0.05, |log2-FC| > 1,
Figure 3A
). Notably, RPL23A and DENND4B exhibited the most significant increase in the CB group (
P
< 0.001). An interaction network of DEPs was developed using the STRING database (
Figure 3B
). Specifically, DEPs with reduced expression in the CB group demonstrated stronger interactions, with apolipoprotein E (APOE) having the most robust interaction with other DEPs, including C1QC, which can inhibit antitumor immunity by modulating macrophages [
20
]. We further examined GO distribution to investigate the biological roles of the upregulated and downregulated DEPs in the CB group. The proteins significantly upregulated in the CB group were primarily associated with immune-related pathways, such as immune response activation, type I IFN-related pathways, positive regulation of T-cell proliferation and activation, positive regulation of TNF production, and antigen processing and presentation (
Figure 3C
). Conversely, significantly downregulated proteins in the CB group were predominantly enriched in complement activation, humoral immune response, immunoglobulin-mediated immune response, and B-cell-mediated immunity (
Figure 3D
). Representative radiologic changes following CAR-GPC3 T-cell infusion are shown in
Figure 3E

Discussion
In this study, we examined alterations in the plasma proteome following CAR-GPC3 T-cell therapy in patients with HCC and identified predictive proteins associated with CB. The results illustrated the comprehensive and dynamic profiles of plasma proteins during CAR-GPC3 T-cell therapy in HCC patients, highlighting the potential of protein liquid biopsy for predicting patient responses to cell therapy.
Using paired plasma samples from patients with HCC undergoing CAR-GPC3 T-cell therapy, we assessed the effects of CAR-T cells on the peripheral plasma proteome. Our results showed that proteins associated with T-cell proliferation and activation significantly increased after CAR-GPC3 T-cell therapy. GNLY, typically expressed by natural killer (NK) and activated T cells, possesses cytolytic activity against tumors [
21
]. LGALS9 has been reported to be associated with dynamic interactions between the immune system and tumor responses to immunotherapy [
22
]. CXCL11 can enhance chemotaxis of activated NK and T cells and promote the infiltration of these immune cells into tumors [
23
]. These proteins significantly increased after the infusion of CAR-GPC3 T cells.
Similarly, studies have shown that CAR T-cell therapy activates T cells in the tumor microenvironment (TME) that are positive for IFN-γ and granzyme B [
24
]. Haydar
et al
. [
25
] also observed that CAR T-cell therapy can alter the tumor immune microenvironment, where the activity of endogenous T cells plays a role in effective antitumor responses. Furthermore, by comparing the baseline plasma proteomes of the CB and NCB groups, we found that the CB group exhibited higher levels of proteins associated with positive regulation of T-cell proliferation and activation. As a small number of activated CAR T cells can stimulate a large number of intratumorally immune cells, the presence of T cells in the tumor prior to CAR T-cell therapy might suggest a primed condition for antitumor immunity triggered by CAR T cells [
24
]. We define the “primed condition” as a tumor state characterized by a pre-existing T-cell infiltrate and a responsive IFN/TNF axis that can be rapidly amplified by CAR-T-derived signals. In our cohort, the baseline enrichment of proteins and GO terms in the CB group, which included positive regulation of T-cell proliferation or activation, type I IFN response, and TNF production, aligns with this primed state. While this condition likely facilitates the intratumoral amplification of infused CAR-T cells, it is an important but non-exclusive determinant of efficacy. This is evidenced by the lack of association between clinical covariates and outcomes, in contrast to the significant prognostic power of plasma proteins. Additionally, we observed that proteins downregulated after CAR T-cell therapy were associated with humoral immunity, which is consistent with previous findings. Walti
et al
. [
26
] conducted a prospective study on humoral immunogenicity after CAR T-cell therapy and found that vaccine immunogenicity was relatively diminished in recipients. Dhakal
et al
. [
27
] also reported low seroconversion rates in patients receiving CAR T-cell therapy after vaccination. Reduced humoral immunity highlights the need for increased vigilance regarding potential infections in CAR T-cell therapy recipients, and caution is advised when vaccinating these patients.
We also observed the effects of CAR-GPC3 T cells on cytokine-related proteins, which are associated with clinical advantages for these patients. CAR-GPC3 T cells could increase the proteins associated with the response to type I IFN, and the upregulated baseline plasma proteins in the CB group were also part of the type I IFN-related pathway. It has been documented that IFN-γ produced by CAR T cells is crucial for maintaining the cytotoxicity of cytokine-activated T cells and tumor regression [
28
]. Type I IFN-γ plays multiple roles in antitumor immunity, including modulation of neo-angiogenesis, immune recruitment and activation, and tumor immunogenicity [
29–31
]. Although the role of IFN-γ in natural immune responses has been extensively studied, its function in CAR T cells remains unclear. During CAR T-cell therapy, IFN-γ can maintain the cytotoxic potential of CAR T cells
in situ
[
28
]. Additionally, Ma
et al
. [
32
] discovered that IFN-γ produced by CAR T cells was vital for enabling an antigen-spreading response, which was propagated through a positive feedback loop with IL-12. Based on the GO results in this study, we inferred that a high level of baseline IFN-γ could promote the activation and cytotoxicity of CAR-GPC3 T cells and that CAR-GPC3 T cells could also enhance the expression of IFN-γ, potentially forming a positive feedback loop.
IFN-γ plays a crucial role in promoting the activation of both innate and adaptive immunity [
33
] and in maintaining T-cell cytotoxicity and mobility [
34
]. In the context of CAR-T cell therapy, studies have demonstrated that IFN-γ enhances CAR-T cell killing efficacy. Specifically,
in vitro
comparisons of cytotoxicity between wild-type CAR-T cells and those deficient in IFN-γ (IFN-γ
−/−
) and/or IFN-γ receptor 1 (IFNGR1
−/−
) against tumor cells revealed that the absence of IFN-γ signaling significantly impaired cytotoxicity [
32
,
35
]. This reduction in cytotoxicity was associated with diminished antigen presentation capacity and reduced dendritic cell (DC) infiltration. Moreover, our previous experiments demonstrated that co-incubation of CAR-GPC3 T cells with various HCC tumor cell lines
in vitro
resulted in significantly increased IFN-γ expression within 8–24 h [
36
,
37
]. Consistently, upon injecting CAR-GPC3 T cells into murine HCC models, we observed elevated systemic IFN-γ levels in the blood several days postinjection [
38
]. These collective findings from our prior work confirm that CAR-GPC3 T-cell activation enhances IFN-γ production, which not only contributes to direct tumor killing but also initiates a broader immune-activating loop.
In addition to IFN-γ, CAR-GPC3 T cells also increased the expression of proteins related to TNF production, which were also enriched in the pretreatment plasma of the CB group. We also noted that plasma proteins that were significantly associated with PFS were involved in the TNF-mediated signaling pathway. The secretion of cellular inflammatory cytokines, including TNFα, can counteract the immunosuppressive microenvironment and enhance the infiltration of CAR T cells and cytotoxic T cells, supporting our findings that higher pretreatment levels of TNF production-related proteins indicate the clinical benefits of CAR-GPC3 T-cell treatment [
39
]. Furthermore, the production of IFN-γ and TNF-α can indicate the effective activation of CAR-T cells [
40
]. In summary, proteins altered by CAR-GPC3 T-cell therapy could be broadly categorized into two groups: those involved in remodeling TME and those indicative of systemic inflammation. The TME-remodeling signature was characterized by elevated levels of CXCL11, GNLY, and LGALS9, alongside upregulated pathways related to type I IFN response, T-cell proliferation or activation, TNF production, and antigen processing or presentation. Conversely, the systemic inflammation signature was marked by the downregulation of complement and immunoglobulin-related pathways, as well as decreased levels of HAMP and TAC3, suggesting a shift in the systemic inflammatory state.
In terms of PFS, we further found that proteins associated with prognosis were also involved in PD-L1 expression and the PD-1 checkpoint pathway. It has been found that the overexpression of PD-L1 on tumor cells can hinder the effector function of CAR T cells. This impairment can be overcome by PD-1 blockade [
41
]. However, tumor recurrence still occurs after cessation of PD-1 blockade therapy, suggesting the necessity for repeated antibody administration to sustain effectiveness. Researchers are investigating combination therapies involving CAR T cells and checkpoint blockades to enhance the efficacy of CAR T-cell therapy through both extrinsic and intrinsic cell approaches, such as the use of lentiviral vectors to induce the expression of anti-carbonic CAR and anti-PD-L1 antibodies in primary human T cells. Clinical trials are also underway to evaluate the effectiveness of combining checkpoint inhibitors with CAR-T cells [
42
]. Our findings also suggest that PD-1 blockade could potentially improve the prognosis of HCC patients undergoing CAR-GPC3 T-cell therapy, which can be validated in future clinical trials.
Investigating protein biomarkers aids in recognizing crucial pathophysiological indicators that have the potential to significantly improve precision medicine. Nonetheless, advancements have been hindered by the absence of technologies that offer reliable sensitivity, specificity, and high throughput. In this study, we employed liquid chromatography-tandem MS utilizing plasma protein corona formed on zeolite NaY to comprehensively map the plasma proteome [
15
]. Proteomic data obtained from MS can be combined with machine learning algorithms to identify potential proteomic markers for assessing treatment effectiveness and survival outcomes in patients with cancer [
14
]. MS enables detailed examination of intact proteins from peripheral blood samples using a top-down approach, facilitating easy integration into routine clinical practice.
Indeed, growing evidence supports that plasma proteomics can capture TME-associated changes, especially when there is active immunologic engagement within the tumor. In a comprehensive longitudinal cohort including lung cancer and lymphoma patients treated with anti-PD1 immunotherapy, Tan
et al
. [
43
] reported that blood plasma proteomic dynamics closely mirror proteomic changes observed within tumor tissue and associated immune organs, which indicates that plasma can serve as a non-invasive window into TME-driven immune activity. Moreover, integrated “plasma-to-tumor” proteomics revealed 30%–45% overlap between plasma and resected tumor proteins in glioblastoma patients, indicating that plasma reliably reflects critical pathways active within the TME [
44
]. In this study, all enrolled HCC patients had confirmed GPC3-positive tumors, and CAR-GPC3 T cells were infused with the aim of eliciting a tumor-localized immune reaction. Thus, we infer that the dynamic plasma protein alterations are not only systemic immune reflection but also highly indicative of TME engagement for the following reasons: (i) the timing and trajectory of changes coincide with expected CAR-T activation dynamics; and (ii) the specific proteins identified, such as IFN-γ, TNF-α, and CXCL11, are well-known markers of TME inflammation and T-cell recruitment.
Moreover, we identified distinct categories of plasma proteins with potential clinical relevance: (i) treatment-associated proteins (e.g. GNLY, LGALS9, CXCL11, HAMP, and TAC3) that reflect dynamic immune responses following CAR-GPC3 T-cell therapy; and (ii) proteins associated with survival outcomes. These protein groups may serve as valuable leads for future biomarker development. Treatment-associated proteins could be used to monitor pharmacodynamic responses, whereas survival-associated proteins may provide prognostic insights or inform risk stratification strategies. Further validation in larger, independent cohorts is required to determine their clinical utility.
We acknowledge several limitations in this study. First, the limited sample size and the fact that it was conducted at a single center may have affected the consistency and reliability of the results. It is necessary to validate these findings externally using larger groups. The proteins and pathways associated with therapeutic efficiency identified in our study align with those identified in previous studies, which, to some extent, supports the reliability of our findings. Second, as we gathered these samples from clinical trials of CAR-GPC3 T-cell therapy in patients with HCC, it remains to be determined whether the results are applicable to other cellular therapies for different cancers. Third, the TME might have a more significant impact on the effectiveness of CAR-T cell therapy in solid tumors than in blood cancer. It is clinically important to investigate whether changes in the plasma proteome can indicate remodeling of the TME during CAR T-cell therapy in solid tumors, which could potentially broaden the clinical use of liquid biopsy.
In conclusion, this study uncovered a defined plasma protein pattern accompanying CAR-GPC3 T-cell therapy in HCC, which featured increases in TME-remodeling proteins like CXCL11 and GNLY. Critically, CB and survival outcomes were tied not to clinical variables, but to baseline levels of specific plasma proteins. These findings point to a practical plasma protein panel for stratifying and monitoring HCC patients receiving CAR-GPC3 T-cell therapy.
